protocol_description: Verbatim copy of the pinned SCiEL example `examples/alphaevolve_math_problems/tammes_problem` (commit da80706f98f9); the evaluator, seed program and configuration are the upstream files. README.upstream.md is the upstream README when one exists.
name: SCiEL: Tammes problem with 13 sphere points
description: Place 13 points on the unit sphere maximizing the smallest Euclidean separation.

sources.locator: evaluate and helper validators at immutable commit

limitations: Source-inspected SCiEL example; not a reproduced paper result.
The original evaluator and baseline are fetched at the immutable source commit; no upstream implementation is silently repaired.
The upstream evaluator provides no independently trusted validity boolean; a finite returned score remains unverified.

papers.title: SCiEL — Scientific Closed-loop Evolutionary Learning: benchmark examples

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Maximize the minimum pairwise separation of thirteen points on the sphere.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: This is a precise extremal geometry problem about spherical packing. The research establishes an optimal arrangement, and the local task searches the same thirteen-point objective.

papers.title: The strong thirteen spheres problem
papers.task_relation: The paper solves the Tammes problem for thirteen sphere points by a computer-assisted proof. The local task optimizes this same fixed-cardinality arrangement; it is a numerical construction task and does not itself reproduce the proof.
papers.primary_goal: Determine and prove the optimal arrangement of thirteen nonoverlapping spheres touching a central sphere.

science_relevance.reason: Primary research addresses the underlying problem directly; scientific importance does not rely on the agent/framework paper.
science_relevance.definition: A task is important to science when it addresses a substantive scientific or real-world problem, and a cited research paper's main objective is to solve that problem or advance understanding of it. The evidence must explain why the problem matters and how the local task represents it. Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
